title: Securing Human Potential and Freedom in the Age of Agentic AI

segments.text: >> ANNOUNCER: Please welcome Chief Executive
Officer and co-founder SentinelOne, Tomer Weingarten.
>> TOMER WEINGARTEN: Hey everybody.
I am very excited to be here today in such a pivotal time
for humanity and for our industry.
It's definitely a very, very unique point in time
for all of us.
We are standing at the edge of one of the most profound
shifts in human history, and the defining question of our
lifetime is this.
How do we ensure that humans thrive in the era of AI?
We are investing trillions of dollars to advance
artificial intelligence, but how much have we invested
intentionally, deliberately, in making ourselves smarter,
in upgrading human intelligence?
I don't mean hiring more people.
I don't mean buying more tools.
I mean actually making human beings more capable, sharper,
more resilient, and better equipped to navigate the world
we are building.
The honest answer is almost nothing.
And I'm not here today to debate whether AI will displace jobs.
I'm not here to hype up AI Agents.
You've heard about all the claws, and I'm certainly not
here to talk about yet another wave of software disruption.
I'm here to talk about something much bigger, something far more
important, the future of human intelligence.
Every major era in history was defined by a tool that changed
what humans could do.
But AI is fundamentally different.
It changes what we can do, but it changes how we think.
It changes what we trust, and what we see first,
and what we act on next.
AI is not just altering the tools we use.
It is altering the very conditions under which human
beings form judgment.
And when the environment of human cognition changes,
civilization changes with it.
This is not simply a new technology.
It's a new stage of human existence and
of human consciousness.
For hundreds of years, thousands of years,
the human brain evolved at the speed of biology.
But in just the last few decades, the framework of
human thought have changed.
Our perception, our knowledge, the very way we form opinions
today, they are tethered to a digital extension of ourselves.
This is where we must also recognize that AI is
not just tethered to our individual minds,
it is mediating our relationships with each other.
When AI curates what we see and believe,
it risks fracturing the shared reality that communities
like ours rely on to function.
Many of us like to say that AI is augmenting our thinking.
That's the optimistic reading.
The honest reading, it is quietly replacing parts
of our thinking.
And we are not even tracking what we are losing.
We are beginning to outsource our cognition to machines.
And this shift affects every single person in this room,
whether you build AI systems or you've never written a
single line of code.
Let me paint a picture of the reality we are actually living
in right now.
AI is writing code, refactoring applications,
provisioning infrastructure, making operational decisions,
driving cars, running our factories, and soon it will
be controlling the robots in our homes.
The very infrastructure of our lives is managed and
influenced by AI.
But it goes even deeper.
It has become the lens through which we consume reality.
It is shaping what we know, what we believe,
and increasingly what we accept is right or wrong.
We have crossed a threshold.
We no longer just use AI as a tool.
We are living inside AI-generated environments built
and maintained by machines.
We have entered a fundamentally different
relationship with technology and it requires a fundamentally
different approach to how and what we need to secure.
Because for the first time in human history,
we are deploying systems at a global scale that no
human fully understands.
This changes the entire concept of verification,
authenticity, intent, and what they mean.
We are no longer dealing with a completely new attack surface.
We are facing an entirely new threat paradigm.
When machines mediate our code, infrastructure,
information, interfaces, and decisions, the attack surface
is no longer bound by endpoints or
identities or clouds.
Traditional infrastructure and tools do not form intent.
AI does.
The battlefield has expanded far beyond the digital realm.
It now includes interpretation, trust,
confidence, decision- making, reality itself.
And that is the breakthrough insight for our industry.
In a machine-generated world, attackers don't
only target systems.
They target the human judgment operating inside those systems.
And they are also targeting societal trust.
When reality itself becomes the attack surface, the goal of an
adversary is often to break down community cohesion.
A fractured community cannot defend itself.
And AI did not just help attackers.
It changed who can attack, how they attack,
and what they attack, and the speed in which defense and
attack actually operate.
And on the defense side, we are deploying AI systems that
no human fully understands, AI-generated code that can't
be audited by human eyes, and infrastructure provisioned by
agents making decisions faster than we can even review them.
We've moved from trust but verify to trust because
we can't verify.
Now, pair this new paradigm and velocity with an industry
that is under-invested in human capability for decades.
Alert-driven detect and respond security was built for
a world where human analysts could actually
keep pace with the threat.
That world is gone.
I want to be honest about our industry.
We build incredible technology, detection engines,
AI-powered analytics, automated response.
Our tools have never been more powerful.
But here's the trap.
As we automate more of our defense,
something subtle happens.
The humans in the loop begin to lose the instinct and
pattern recognition skills that made them effective in
the first place.
We become supervisors of systems we no longer fully understand.
We trust AI to detect threats, trust AI
to triage, to remediate.
We delegate action.
And over time, we lose the ability to catch the things
AI gets wrong.
This is not an argument against AI in security.
AI is essential.
It is the only way to operate at the speed and scale that
modern threats demand.
But AI without proper human investment creates a system
that is fast and capable, but also fundamentally brittle
because when the machine gets it wrong, and it will be wrong,
who catches it?
If you are making critical security decisions on four
hours of sleep, three energy drinks, and chronic stress,
you are the vulnerability, despite the best intentions.
For a long time, our industry has obsessed over building
better cockpits, while putting unprepared pilots in the seat.
At some point, the answer isn't a better cockpit.
It's a better pilot.
This means we can't just take legacy cybersecurity tools and
continue to automate them.
We don't need a faster hamster wheel.
We need a completely new architecture.
So how do we create a security model capable of
governing autonomous systems?
How do we govern action itself when agency is distributed
across humans and machines?
What cybersecurity must govern now is not just systems,
but agency itself.
Human and machine operating at speed with consequence.
This is why the doctrine we need is verifiable agency.
And the doctrine is simple: speed, evidence,
agency, boundaries, attribution, and accountability.
If a system cannot act in time, it does not matter.
If it cannot show the evidence behind its actions,
it cannot be trusted.
If it cannot act when needed, it cannot defend.
If it cannot stay within boundaries,
it cannot be governed.
If its action cannot be attributed,
authority disappears.
And if accountability is lost, control is an illusion.
What makes this paradigm possible is one foundational
capability: continuous behavioral visibility.
The ability to observe, understand, and verify how
agency is being exercised across humans and machines
in real time.
In many ways, this has been our thesis from the beginning.
More than a decade ago, SentinelOne was founded on a
pioneering conviction that behavior is the decisive signal,
the only reliable way to distinguish the benign
from the malicious at machine speed.
Today, our patented behavioral AI is deployed at global scale.
And now, we are extending that same principle into the
age of AI itself, using behavioral intelligence to make
autonomous action verifiable, governable, and trustworthy.
What that means in practice is that AI
operates at machine speed, detecting, correlating,
acting in milliseconds.
But every autonomous action is traceable, auditable,
and overridable by a human.
AI provides the scale, speed, pattern recognition,
and humans provide the judgment, the context,
and the ethical guardrails.
These ethical guardrails are the community imperative.
The humans in the loop aren't just protecting
an enterprise network, they are acting as representatives
of human values and societal norms.
Verifiable agency isn't just a technical doctrine;
it's a social contract ensuring machines
remain accountable to human communities.
But there's another key question here.
How do we ensure humans stay in charge of such systems?
The future belongs to a new paradigm where machines
execute at speed, evidence stays traceable,
and humans remain accountable for outcomes:
a genuine co-evolution where one makes the other stronger
and none can succeed alone.
We are investing trillions into artificial intelligence.
It is time we apply the exact same rigor and resources in
elevating human intelligence.
The human mind remains the most formidable processing
engine on the planet.
But like any system, it needs training, it needs maintenance,
and we need to train our people to think,
not just to operate tools.
Red team exercises that sharpen human instincts,
not just test automated defenses.
War games that force decision-making
under uncertainty.
Career paths that reward deep expertise
and adversarial thinking, not just certifications.
And for the leaders in this room, this means encouraging
cognitive diversity in decision-making, breaking the
pattern of groupthink, and actively cultivating people
who challenge the consensus, because AI will
never do that for you.
And we need to sharpen judgment, think critically,
demand reality, verifiability.
AI should be a thought gym for your people.
Use it to challenge their assumptions, use it to stress
test their reasoning, use it to accelerate learning.
The moment your team stops verifying AI output,
the moment they accept that its conclusions without engaging
their own judgment, they have stopped exercising.
And cognitive atrophy is just as real as physical atrophy.
It is our responsibility to invest in the human element.
Our brains are biological systems, and we must start
treating them as critical infrastructure.
As an industry, we must invest in the operating conditions of
our people's minds with the same rigor we apply to the
uptime of our servers, their skills, their rest,
their physical health, their mental resilience,
even their nutrition.
Think of it not as a wellness initiative,
but as a security capability.
Let's recognize and break old patterns,
be open-minded, get uncomfortable.
The people who thrive in this new era will be the ones who
use AI to hone human discernment and never
to surrender it.
As an industry, we are no longer defending just enterprises.
We are helping preserve the conditions for
trustworthy digital reality.
We are the keepers of what comes next.
If AI is going to shape the future of human potential,
then security must shape the future of AI and ensure that
AI is a force for good.
The decisions we all make about how humans and AI work
together and share agency will determine whether
this era amplifies humanity or diminishes it.
We have spent the last several years accelerating
artificial intelligence.
The next decade must also be about advancing
human intelligence, not as a slogan, but through serious
investment in neuroscience, neuroplasticity, brain health,
and the ethical protection of human agency itself.
Because advancing human intelligence is not just about
making individuals smarter.
It's about strengthening the collective intelligence
of all of us, deepening resilience, and building
communities better equipped to think, adapt, and endure.
This is the defining challenge of our lifetime,
and it all starts and ends with us.
Thank you.
